messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 50-year-old African American plumber married to his high school sweetheart, has been struggling with the aftermath of an assault that occurred six months ago. On that fateful evening, John was making a late-night trip to a client’s home in a part of town he wasn’t familiar with when he encountered three men who demanded money and assaulted him. The violence left deep physical and emotional scars. Since the attack, John has found himself only feeling safe within a limited number of places—his home and his immediate neighborhood. Even there, he remains hyper-vigilant, reacting sharply to any unexpected movements around him as if danger lurks just beyond his sight. At night, these fears disrupt his sleep, leading to persistent insomnia that leaves him exhausted during the day. The traumatic event itself haunts John in vivid images and flashes of fragmented memories. Each time he recalls the assault, it is accompanied by an overwhelming sense of guilt, as though he could have done something to prevent it. This inability to articulate what happened further intensifies his distress; the words just don’t come easily when trying to make sense of such a traumatic experience. John’s self-doubt has grown significantly since the assault. He feels no longer capable of performing tasks that once defined him as a skilled plumber, leading to hesitations and anxieties at work. The injustice of what happened to him gnaws at his sense of fairness, leaving him with a deep-seated belief that nothing will be done about it. These negative appraisals have intensified his fear and hypervigilance, creating a cycle where his heightened threat sensitivity is exacerbated by the guilt and self-doubt he experiences. The memory of the assault continues to trigger John’s intense feelings of vulnerability and fear. Whenever he sees something that reminds him of the attack—like dark alleyways or groups of men—he reacts with an immediate surge of anxiety, which in turn reinforces his belief that danger is always close at hand. This reinforcement cycle makes it increasingly difficult for John to venture outside his safe zones. John’s daily work as a plumber has become challenging due to these symptoms. He avoids jobs in unfamiliar neighborhoods and often turns down calls late at night out of fear of another assault. His wife has noticed the changes, worried about both his physical and emotional well-being. Despite her support, John feels increasingly isolated, with his ability to function in daily life diminishing. What finally brought John to seek help was a particularly distressing episode at work where he experienced a panic attack while on a job site. This event left him feeling more incapable than ever and realizing that his fears were starting to control his life. He is most afraid of continuing down this path, but also hopes for the possibility of reclaiming some sense of normalcy and regaining confidence in himself. John’s story illustrates how the interplay between negative appraisals, memory intrusions, and heightened threat sensitivity can create a self-reinforcing cycle that severely impacts his quality of life. He seeks help not only to alleviate his symptoms but also to regain control over his daily functioning and sense of identity as a capable individual.
